On Wednesday there was laid upon the table of the house a petition praying for the passing of an act to incorporate the Morris Finance Corporation. I now beg to move:
That the petition of Gerald Murphy and others of Toronto, Ontario, praying for the passing of an act to incorporate the Morris Finance Corporation, which was presented to the house on the 27th day of May, together with the report of the clerk of petitions thereon, be referred to the select standing committee on standing orders for the purpose of considering the suspension of standing order 92 in relation thereto.
Motion agreed to.

The committee will resume consideration of the following item:
Dairying, including grant of $5,000 to National Dairy Council, $295,000.
And the amendment thereto of Mr. Young.
Would the minister be kind enough to give me the information referred to yesterday afternoon about the rock bottom price reached by butter when the Australian butter was released?
The date when it was mutually agreed to release the Australian butter was April 21. The price of butter on that date was 22 cents a pound.
Did the Australian butter sell at the same price, 22 cents a pound, then?
I do not think I have under my hand any information as to what Australian butter was sold for on that date.

It would be interesting to know at what price the Australian butter was sold when it was released. I understand from the minister that the price cutting warfare took place in Vancouver. I should like to know the price of Australian butter in Vancouver on that date, and also the price of butter in London, England, on the same date.
We have no information as to what Australian butter sold at or as to the price' of butter in London, England on that date.
Would the minister endeavour to get that information?
Yes.
What quantity of Australian butter was released on April 21?

All the Australian butter that was in Canada. On April 21 it was mutually agreed that the Australian butter could be released at less than 32 cents a pound. It was not all put on the market in one day; it was put on the market, I believe, over a period of days. I do not know whether it is all sold yet or not.

The minister does not
know the quantity of butter which was released on that date? That is what I should like to know.	[DOT]
Does the hon. member mean how many pounds of Australian butter were in Canada on that date?
How much was released?
It was all released.
What quantity was in storage at that time?
Approximately 15,000 boxes.

How many pounds in a box?
Svpply-Agriculture*-Dairying
Around fifty pounds.
Did the release apply also to 'butter that was coming to Vancouver and that was not in storage at that moment?

I do not .think there was any butter coming from Australia at that time. By the way, a question came up yesterday and I promised to get information with regard to it. That information I received today from the Department of National Revenue. As regards butter imported from Australia during .the month of April, the information given to me is that no butter from Australia was imported through any port of Canada during April and May of this year.
So what was released was only what arrived in Canada prior to that date?
Yes.

I did not hear all the speech delivered yesterday .by my eloquent and genial friend, the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), but I read it carefully in Hansard. At page 2069 of Hansard he gave figures as to the export of butter by pounds, and said:
We were exporting .twenty-five times less butter at the end of five years than when the treaty became effective.
The figures he gave covered the years from 1925 to 1930, and his statement in that regard might be accurate, but I notice, Mr. Chairman, that he gave other figures as to the imports of butter in pounds for the same years, and in 1929 the amount of butter imported was 35,928,240 pounds, and the price of butter in that year was 38-60, according to the figures which the hon. member himself gave. The amount of butter imported in 1930, according to the hon. member's own figures again, was 38,606,055 pounds, and the price dropped, according to his own figures, to 31 cents a pound. Thus the relationship between the importation in pounds, and the price per pound, was not maintained as compared with the previous year. My hon. friend the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) intervened in the debate at a very appropriate moment with this question:
Mr. Veniot:	Has the hon. member also the
figures of the production and consumption in Canada?
Mr. Hackett:	No.
Mr. Veniot:	Then his argument falls to
the ground. We produced over forty million pounds less than we were able to consume.
Some hon. Members:	Why?
Mr. Hackett: I would point out to the committee that there was every reason for our production of butter to increase during that period because in those years, by reason of legislation hostile to the export of milk and

cream-this is particularly true of the eastern townships, and truer still of the border counties of the eastern townships from which such large quantities of milk and cream were exported to the large centres of New England -exports were greatly curtailed.
Here are the figures of the production and consumption of butter in 1929. I have not the figures for 1930, but I would request the minister to supply them to the committee to-night if possible. The production of butter in 1929, according to a leter written by the chief of the agricultural branch of the bureau of statistics, was 174,724,465 pounds of creamery butter and 90,000,000 pounds of homemade butter; so the total production of creamery and homemade butter in 1929 was 264,724,465 pounds, and the consumption was 299,348,271 pounds. Therefore, butter consumption was that year 34,623,806 pounds more than production. That point is most important. On May 26, at page 2166 of Hansard I asked the Minister of Agriculture this question, and I must congratulate him upon his answer being in accordance with the facts:
Mr. Pouliot: So long as the production of butter in this country is less than the consumption, is it necessary, in order to supply the trade and the public in general, to import butter?
Mr. Weir (Melfort):	Do I understand the
hon. member's question to be this: If the production of butter in Canada is less than the consumption, should we allow the importation of butter ?
Mr. Pouliot: No; is it necessary to import butter from outside?
Mr. Weir (Melfort):	Yes.
There the minister himself admitted that when the consumption was in excess of production, importations had to be made in order to meet the requirements of the public. It is sad that production for any reason should fall below consumption in this country, but one reason for that has already been given, namely, the considerable increase in the tourist traffic during the last few years.
During the last campaign we were told by the Conservative speakers from almost every platform that with a high tariff on butter the price would rise considerably. I was speaking the other day of a minimum of 40 cents a pound. During the campaign the price of butter was 32 cents a pound, and the Conservative speakers said that it should be at least 40 cents a pound. They said that in order to bring butter up to that point, the leader of the Conservative party, if returned to power, would put a tariff of eight cents a pound on butter, which with the 32 cents, which was then the prevailing price, would bring butter up to 40 cents a pound. But in spite of that duty which has been

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
imposed on butter, the price has fallen, to about 20 cents. Practically every Conservative speaker in the rural ridings concluded his speech by saying, "Now, gentlemen," and ladies also, because the ladies were interested in milking the cows, "go home and think of the price you now receive for your butter from the factories." People were reminded in every country place of the prices they were then receiving for butter and were told that when they reached their homes they should by calculation see if the Liberal government had not betrayed their interests. What has happened? The present condition is much worse. What about the betrayal? They were to change the tariff in order to adjust the price of butter but their promise proved to be a myth.

Hon. members have heard a great deal about the Australian treaty. I have in my hand an excerpt from L'Evenement of November 30, 1928. From the first page of this publication I read the following:
The Tories support Mr. Robb, in 1924
The Australian treaty seemed to be doomed when L. J. Ladner rallied a group of Conservatives.
An interesting incident.
The member for Vancouver South reveals the fact at a meeting held in the interest of D. B. Plunkett.
By-election.	*
(Canadian Press Service)
Vancouver, 30.-A summary of the part played by the Conservative party in the House of Commons in connection with the enactment of the Australian treaty by parliament was revealed to us last night by Mr. Leon J. Ladner, federal member for Vancouver South, at a meeting held in the interest of the Conservative candidate for the dominion by-election which was to take place on December 6.
I make this statement, he said, to counteract the false impressions left by government mem-22110-133
bers and other Liberals in their speeches with reference to the stand taken by the Conservative party, in the House of Commons, in connection with this treaty. The treaty at present, in force had its inception in 1924 when a provisional understanding was concluded between the two countries.
The Conservative party held solidly together on its tariff policy. On the night of June 22, four days previous to the prorogation of parliament, the hon. Mr. J. A. Robb presented his Australian treaty. He was greatly criticized. especially by the progressive party led by Mr. Forke. The duties on raisins were the principal pretext involved in their criticism, however the treaty itself was not made a party affair. Each member was free to express his own opinion, whether he considered this measure from the viewpoint of Canada or from that of a particular province.
Just before nine o'clock, in the evening, on June 24, the news, emanating from the government benches, spread in the house that Mr Robb would withdraw the treaty and no further consideration would be given to it at that session. Four minutes later Mr. Robb moved that the committee rise and report progress, which automatically meant the killing of the treaty. Mr. Robb then left the house.
Realizing the importance of the treaty from the viewpoint of British Columbia, I followed Mr. Robb out of the chamber and met him in the lobby. I asked him the reason for such action. He frankly admitted to me that he feared an adverse vote, especially after the stand taken by the Progressives. I replied that it was not a question of party and that a number of Conservatives would support his measure. I then interviewed a number of members and further assured Mr. Robb that, if he would reintroduce his measure, the members that I had just mentioned to him, including myself, would strongly speak in its favour and support it by their votes.
On my suggestion other influential Conservatives, such as Dr. Manion (now Minister of Railways and Canals), spoke to Mr. Robb and confirmed what I had told him. Mr. Robb then assured me that he would again introduce the measure, which he did the following day. The hill was strongly supported by the Conservative party.
I have before me the Gazette, Montreal, of December 3, 1928, corroborating the article I read in French about the declaration made by Mr. L. J. Ladner, a former member from the province of British Columbia. The article is as follows:
Stevens would aid Australian trade.
I would commend this particular article to the attention of my hon. friend from Stan-stead. If he is not in the house undoubtedly he will see my remarks in Hansard. The article continues:
Suggests cancellation of pact with France, if necessary, to help antipodes (by Canadian Press).
Victoria, B.C., December 1.-"The trouble with Canada and Canada's side of the Australian treaty is that the present government has never shown a friendly spirit toward Australia." The Hon. H. H. Stevens, M.P. for

Vancouver Centre, declared here last night in addressing a meeting in support of D. B. Plunkett, Conservative candidate in the approaching Victoria by-election.
Hon. Mr. Stevens went so far as to suggest the cancellation of the French treaty in order to aid Australia.
Canada imports large quantities of wine.
Are not French wines much better than Australian wines?
Let Mr. Robb give to Australia at least the same treatment accorded to France, or, better still, denounce the French treaty, which has been altogether unfavourable to us, or else enlarge the Australian treaty by giving a preference to her in wine.
At that time my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) who, I am pleased to say is in his seat to-day was not satisfied with the Australian treaty, not because it gave too much to Australia but because it did not give enough to Australia.
That is right.

I have another matter to
bring before the committee. I find in La Presse, Montreal, on May 18, 1931, tire statement that the price of butter is so low that butter is used to make soap. After reading this statement I can readily understand how easily my hon. friends to your right, Mr. Chairman, washed their hands of the responsibility for the low price of butter, which is rather easy on account of the fact that butter is used in the manufacture of soap.
What quantity of butter was in storage last year when the high duty was imposed? There was quite a large quantity. On August 1, 1930, there were 32,643,390 pounds of creamery butter in storage, and 944,539 pounds of dairy butter. On September the first, after the Prime Minister had been in power for a few weeks and had repeated that he was going to make good his policy of increasing the tariff on farm commodities, the amount of creamery butter in cold storage was 39,572,168 pounds; about 7,000,000 pounds more than the previous month. I am under the impression, Mr. Chairman, that your constituency is partly a rural constituency surrounding the beautiful city of Fredericton, and consequently you must be familiar with the prices of farm products. No doubt you recall that as soon as the tariff was put on butter the price rose 2 cents a pound-it was the same story as in regard to glass- at that time there was over 40,000,000 pounds of butter in cold storage, so that those who had hoarded that butter made an excess profit in the aggregate of 1800,000. The huge sum 
came out of the pockets of the people for the benefit of the owners of cold storage plants. It is a most serious condition of affairs, because the farmers were deprived of that $800,000.
Who paid that $800,000?
The consumer.
Certainly.

What was the price paid
for the butter that was put into cold storage? I may tell my hon. friend that the cold storage man paid more than 32 cents a pound for that butter, so he did not make anything on the transaction; he lost.
How do you know?

I do not remember the
price of butter at that time, but I do remember very well, and this may be confirmed by looking up the market quotations, that the moment the high tariff of 8 cents a pound became operative the price of cold storage butter went up 2 cents a pound. My hon. friend from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) will not deny the fact that not a single farmer got the slightest share of that 8800,000; it all went into the pockets of the shareholders of those cold storage plants. I have been frequently told that our High Commissioner in London was interested in a dairy syndicate while he was living in this beloved country.
Order.

Let me go further. On
referring to the Parliamentary Guide of this year, I find at page 494 that the Hon. George Stewart Henry, the present premier of Ontario, is president of the Farmers' Dairy Company, Limited, of Toronto. Toronto is not like Fredericton or Riviere du Loup, it is a bigger city, and although there are beautiful parks they have no pastures. It reminds me of something that will please my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins); a great painter frequently expressed the opinion that no landscape could be perfect without cows appearing in it. Unfortunately in the numerous beautiful parks of the city of Toronto there are no cowrs, there are only policemen-and I don't know how the people could get milk from the batons of those guardians of the peace. But certain gentlemen in Toronto control a very large quantity of the butter that comes from the country. Dairy companies such as the Farmers' Dairy

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
Company, Limited, of Toronto, buy milk from the farmers at a poor price and when through the tariff they get any pecuniary advantage they keep the money in their pockets; the farmers see nothing of it. I think this is a shame, because the tariff was made, not to help the rich people who control the sale of milk, butter, cheese and other dairy products, but to help the farmers themselves. I remember distinctly at the special session last September the Prime Minister said that the tariff amendments he was then putting through were intended to help the producer. Well, the farmer is the producer. The man who lives in a big mansion in Toronto is not a producer; it is the poor man who lives in the country and milks his cows-he furnishes the supply of milk out of which those city magnates get richer and richer and benefit by the tariff and the producer gets no advantage from it.

Last night the hon. Minister of Agriculture asked me where I got the figures I then quoted, and I told him that I would let him have the source of my authority this afternoon, that I was speaking from memory at the moment. I have in my hands a statement from the bureau of statistics, internal trade branch, from which it appears that for the first five months 'of 1930 the average wholesale price of creamery No. 1 butter at Montreal was 37 cents, while the average wholesale price for the same month of creamery extra at New York was 36.3 cents a pound.
That is the average for the five months?

Yes. I can give it month by
month:

That was the basis of the statement I made last night to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) and to the hon, minister. Its accuracy, was challenged by the former, and, as I understood, doubted at least by the minister. The point perhaps is not of very great importance, but, as I said last night I would produce my authority this afternoon, I have now done so.

I was not doubting the hon. gentleman's statement at all, I was just comparing it with the information we have on the average monthly wholesale jobbing prices of creamery butter for Montreal and New York. The Department of Agriculture, dairy and cold storage branch, Ottawa, gives the prices of Canadian butter for January and February higher than for the New York market, but not for the next three months.

I have
just one observation to make. I recall very definitely and distinctly that the right hon. Prime Minister and hon. gentlemen opposite during the recent campaign guaranteed the people of Canada that the imposition of tariffs would protect the consumer as well as the producer. I also recall, sir, that during the special session, when the special legislation was brought down in this parliament, that pledge was repeated by the right hon. Prime Minister and by the members of his administration. Last night we had produced in the committee a most singular document, a very much lauded letter from the president of the National Dairy Council of Canada, the production of which seemed to move my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce to a state of frothy indignation. I desire again to place on Hansard one paragraph from that letter, which appeals at page 2089 of Hansard:
All of this production received the full benefit of the artificial price level which thus resulted in an extra return to the producers of about $7,000,000. This, of course, came from the consumer's pocket direct, and the consumer in addition paid the extra ten cents on the relatively small amount of Australian butter which entered the country during the period in question.
I wish to repeat that I am in favour of every possible assistance that can be rendered to the dairy industry throughout the Dominion of Canada, but I say that when you try to assist the producing dairy industry at the expense of the consuming Canadian public, it is a false assistance and a breach of the pledges made by hon. gentlemen opposite during the special session of parliament.
Could the hon. gentleman tell us how we could help them without raising the price of butter?

That
was your problem. My point is that the pledges made by the hon. gentleman, and the policies he supported during the special
Supply-A gricullure-Dairying

session, have been falsified by the letter produced last evening by the Minister of Agriculture and lauded by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

Does the hon. gentleman
think the people in this country would swallow any such stuff as that? Surely they must have some sense.

Let me say that as a farmer I have listened with more than the usual amount of amusement to the debate which has been going on for about three days on the one question of whether or not we shall vote the sum of S5.00Q to the National Dairy Council of Canada, so that they may carry on during the coming year the wonderful work they have done in years gone by.
I do not think that is the issue; the whole vote is in question.

If the ex-Minister of Agriculture will just keep quiet for a few moments, I should like to continue my remarks. I am very glad he is the ex-Minister of Agriculture. Any man whose policy during the last nine years did for the dairy industry of Canada what his policy has done might well keep quiet. For nine years the hon. member for Melville, the ex-Minister of Agriculture, was like the proverbial ostrich, with his head buried in the sand and his wrong end sticking up. That end was never meant to think with.
Why do you compare him with an ostrich? He has no plumage.

I am coming to you next, and I may as well check you up right now. When this debate opened the hon. member for-Pouliot, is it, or the hon. member for Temiseouata, which sounds about the same- was the one man who seemed to have more to say about the dairy industry, and with regard to butter, cream and agriculture, than anyone else. At once I came to the conclusion that the hon. member was an honest-to-goodness farmer; he looked like one, anyway. Imagine my surprise, Mr. Chairman, when yesterday I turned up the Parliamentary Guide and found that the hon. member for Temiseouata was nothing more or less than a lawyer. Not only that, but he writes books on law, according to the Parliamentary Guide. I tried my best and racked my brain to find out where I would place 'him on a farm, especially a dairy farm, and after a good deal of thought and study I found a place for him; I found something on a dairy farm which the hon. gentleman resembles very much in one respect at least. I refer to the horn flies on the cows. Any farmer as well 
acquainted with cows and agriculture as I am, knows that about six o'clock in the evening, when you bring the cows into the barn to milk them, they are infested with swarms of horn flies. The hon. member for Temiseouata resembles them in this respect, in that the more you try to shoo them off the thicker they seem to get. The more you try to shoo him off from making a speech on something about which he knows nothing, the more speeches he makes. During this debate he has given us figures by the mile and speeches .by the acre, but they have led us nowhere.
Now let me say, Mr. Chairman, that some years ago Canada enjoyed a very enviable position indeed as far as dairying was concerned. There was a time in the history of Canada when every year we were supplying the British market with creamery butter, of wonderful quality, in immense quantities. We were going along very nicely indeed, and there was nothing to interrupt our progress except the former Minister of Agriculture, the hon. member for Melville. He interrupted it very violently indeed. The government of which he was a member brought in the Australian treaty, the terms of which were extended to New Zealand, and thereby hangs a tale. That was the beginning of all our trouble. The farmers of Canada saw that a neighbouring country was getting the benefit of the Canadian market, and dairying in Canada declined to such an extent that we lost out on our export trade. We lost the footing we had already gained on the British market, and let me tell the hon. member that it is very much easier to lose trade of this kind than to build it up.-
We are endeavouring to build up that export trade again. When this government came into power we saw to it that the farmers of Canada were given a fair deal as far as dairying was concerned. We shut out, to a great extent at least, the products of our -competitors, and if nothing unforeseen had occurred to-day we would be getting back on our feet by degrees, building up our export trade together with our production in Canada, but what has happened? Production has come along faster than either consumption or the export trade. That was very well pointed out last evening by the hon. member for Red Deer, and let me say that I always like to hear the hon. member for Red Deer speak, because he has something sane and sensible to tell us when he does speak. Now we have turned our attention to dairying more quickly than we should have done under normal conditions by reason of the fact that

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
wheat prices in western Canada were extremely low. And the farmers of western Canada turned their attention to this industry too quickly. There is another thing which is to a great extent responsible for the increased production of the present time and that is the mild winter we have had throughout Canada and the exceptionally cheap feed which we have had to feed to the dairy cow.
Let me say this-and this is in connection with the dairy council, because it is a part of their work; I might as well point out right here that you cannot build up an export trade in butter, you cannot build up an export trade in any other farm commodity, unless you have the very best that you can possibly produce along these lines. We in eastern Canada have, I believe, done very well in this direction through the action and the encouragement, the knowledge and information which we have had on the part of the National Dairy Council. Through these means we have been attending to the quality and grade of our dairy products. But I find that this has not been the case in western Canada. The hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly), whether we realized it or not, whether the hon. gentleman himself was aware of the fact or not, really gave us more information along this line last night than anyone else whom I, at least, have heard speak. I wish to quote just a word or two from Hansard of yesterday reporting what the hon. member for Willow Bunch said:
111 western Canada to-day it is not the creamery butter, but the dairy butter that counts. Many of our farmers are so far away from the market they are not in a position to have their cream shipped to the creamery. As a result they are concerned only with dairy butter.
Do hon. members stop to think just what that means to the section of country concerned? Let us imagine now a township or a country district. The people have round about them a number of farms,-fifty, seventy-five or a hundred. In the village they have a store or perhaps two. Heretofore these farmers have been wheat growers. They despised the look of a cow, let alone the trouble of milking it. But when their wheat business was shot to pieces, as it has been, unfortunately, during the last year-though I believe it will come back again-they immediately turned their attention to milking cows. They thought they were engaging in dairying, but. they were not. For let me tell you that milking cows and making butter at home and then taking it to the village grocer is about as far removed from intelligent dairying as the sun is from the earth; and never in
any way can you build up an export trade with such a line of farming as that-nor will anything destroy the domestic market more readily. What would you expect the storekeeper to say when a hundred different people, who heretofore have not been making butter at all, flock in with a hundred different samples of butter of various makes, different in grade, different in flavour and different in every other respect? What would you expect a country grocer to say to those people? What would he do with the butter? He could not eat it nor could he ship it to the towns, because it is not of uniform grade. And so far as export is concerned, it is worse than useless.
Our Minister of Agriculture has been asked for an agricultural policy. Let me say to some agricultural sections of Canada that the first thing they need to get is intelligent agriculture. Then the Minister of Agriculture will give them a policy. But a system of agriculture that puts you into wheat to-day, into butter to-morrow and into hogs the next day is a pretty hard line of agriculture for any Minister of Agriculture to keep pace with. It is pretty hard to evolve any policy that will be of any assistance to people engaged in such work.
I would say, with respect to the Minister of Agriculture, that he occupies possibly the most important portfolio after that of Finance, and at the same time one which it is hardest to administer. I have heard an old fanner down homo say that he was durned if he would keep a hired man around the place except to blame things on if things went wrong. That is about the position the Minister of Agriculture occupies in relation to hon. gentlemen opposite. If it does not rain, it is his fault; if it rains too much, he is to blame. If you are short of butter, that is his fault, and if you have too much, he did not regulate things properly. That is the whole story. In eastern Canada, I believe, we are giving the Minister of Agriculture very little trouble indeed, and if he were to tell his experience I believe he would say the same; because for generations we have been following one steady policy, one line of agriculture. We are easy to deal with. When the price of butter is low, we pocket our loss, and when it is high we take our profits and say nothing about it. It is easy to handle such a situation.

May I ask the hon.
gentleman a question?

You may, and if I can answer it I will; if not, I will tell you so.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

Will the hon. gentleman explain why, during the last ten years, since I have been in this house, all the members from the maritime provinces have been always complaining about conditions in that part of the country?
Were they?
Yes.
Well, I was not here to hear them.
You are here as a result of those complaints.
I can assure the hon. gentleman that we hear very few complaints in the maritime provinces.
What about the Duncan commission?

Well, the Duncan commission was all right. But I am not going to be sidetracked by my hon. friend. I may tell him, however, so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, that they cannot register as many complaints to the square inch as I have heard from western members this winter.
Some of them.

Well, yes; there are some
good fellows among them. Now, Mr. Chairman, we are here to-day not to play to the gallery nor to make long speeches. Such speeches are utterly useless to those who are looking for an improved quality of butter and better prices. What we are here for now is to decide whether we will or will not vote the sum of $5,000 for the National Dairy Council to carry on their work. In eastern Canada we regard the National Dairy Council as a very important body, and I should not for one moment have the bravery to go on any platform in that part of the dominion, whether at an agricultural or at a political meeting, or a meeting of any other kind in which farmers were concerned, and advocate doing away with the National Dairy Council.
Who is advocating it?

I believe the hon. member
for Weyburn himself moved a resolution to the effect that the money which will enable the council to carry on their work for the coming year be not voted. If that is not doing away with the National Dairy Council, I should like to know what it means. And let me tell the hon. member for Weyburn here and now that his resolution will make very good reading for Tory politicians when the next federal election comes round. Let us act sensibly. Let us get on with our work.

Let us have done with this foolishness and pass the estimate as it has been passed every year for possibly the last twenty years. It is not different this year from what it was before. The items that the Minister of Agriculture has under his hand follow very closely the items that were voted in the house for the ex-Minister of Agriculture during the last nine years.

They turned around and said, "Your factories are closed; you are shut out of the United States market, and look what the King government has done to the dairy industry through the New Zealand treaty." The farmers of those constituencies believed that story, and voted Conservative. That is the reason why we have some hon. members opposite representing those constituencies to-day. That could not be attributed to the importations of butter from New Zealand; it was due altogether to the United States tariff against our exports of fresh milk and cream.
That disposes of the theory which my hon. friend from Stanstead advanced last night. Then another hon. gentleman said that our cattle population had fallen off, and he stated this was due to the Liberal policy. I want to say that the moment the American tariff went up and American farmers and dairymen saw prospects of our milk and cream being shut out, they came to Canada and began to buy up some of our stock. It was the best thing in the world for the dairymen of this Dominion that they were able to sell their cattle to those American farmers at that time at a good price. Since this government came into power a cow is not worth milking, and if our farmers had not been able to ship these cattle to the United States, at a good price, they would have had them on their hands to-day and would have received no benefit from them. Another point brought up by the ex-Minister of Agriculture was that the tuberculin test took a very heavy toll of the cattle all over this dominion.
Some hon. members have siuggested that immediately the farmers saw something looming up which promised a profit, they switched to dairying over night. No reasonable or intel-
ligent person will accept that theory. You cannot switch to dairying over night. If dairying is coming back, and if to-day we are producing more butter than we need in Canada, that improvement must have been in progress for the last three or four years. You cannot produce over night a dairy herd from which you can obtain milk that will give cream and butter of exportable quality. Such a herd must be built up over a number of years. And the reason we are producing milk to-day and exporting butter .to the United Kingdom is that during the last few years of Liberal regime, under the capable Minister of Agriculture who was in office in that period, the dairy herds of Canada were steadily built up. The result is that to-day we are producing all the butter we need for our own uses and are also in a position to export a surplus to the United Kingdom.
The serious feature of this policy which our hon. friends opposite have introduced is this: it is a double-edged sword; it cuts both ways. Our friends have stated that they were going to build up the dairy industry of Canada and put our dairy farmers on easy street, and the moment the people took them at their word and accepted that policy, the government and the manufacturers association had the dairy farmers in their hands. They were able to squeeze them like a sponge, because they said to the dairy farmers, "You cannot expect a policy of protection for your dairy products and at the same time refuse protection for manufactured articles ".
Now, the moment this 8 cents a pound duty is imposed on New Zealand1 butter we find that our export trade with that country drops off by almost one-half. This morning I obtained from the bureau of statistics the figures for the last three years, from April 1, 1928, to April 30, 1931. Under our agreement with New Zealand, our trade with that country progressed by leaps and bounds. In April of the fiscal year 1928-29 our exports to New Zealand amounted to $704,871, and at the end of March of that same year they had increased to $2,182,788.
I wish to ask the hon. gentleman a question. Is he or is he not in favour of the New Zealand and Australian trade agreements?

It is for the hon. gentleman to draw his own conclusions from my remarks. The treaty built up a wonderful trade between this country and New Zealand, and I am sure that the manufacturers of Canada must have appreciated that fact. The automobile business made rapid strides, as hon. members know. But everyone knew that

the imposition of that 8 cent duty would not help Canadian farmers. Perhaps the hon. gentleman who asked me that question will answer one which I will put to him: Of what benefit has that duty of 8 cents been to the dairymen of Canada?

Statements were made
during the election campaign-I do not wish to refer to this, but the hon. member brought it up-that when we got into power the price of butter would be higher than the price that then prevailed; and it would be to-day if we were not producing so much butter.

I have my hon. ifriend
where I want him. He admits that they did promise the people of the country that they would increase the price of butter.
I did not. I said that what we said was that the price of butter, if we were returned to power, would be higher than the price would be under Liberal administration.
The hon. member's party said it would, and now they are in power I would ask the hon. gentleman that question again: Is the price higher now than when they were making those speeches?
That is a different question.

Oh, it is a different question; I knew the hon. gentleman would not like to answer that question, because we find that the price of butter is 10 cents lower than it was then. Now let me go on with the figures I was quoting. In the year 192930 our exports to New Zealand had increased to the sum of 119,166,488, and that most gratifying state of affairs prevailed until last October. In the month of October of the fiscal year 1930-31 our exports amounted to SI,340,998; that was for the month of October alone. But what happened the moment the duty was put on butter? Immediately upon the imposition of the duty on New Zealand butter our exports to New Zealand fell off, for in the month of November of last year -the very next month after we had shipped over $1,340,000-we find that our exports amounted to just $846,728. In other words, there was a loss of almost $1,000,000 per month to the export trade of this country, while there was absolutely no corresponding benefit to Canadian dairymen. And I will defy any hon. gentleman opposite to stand up in this house at this moment and declare that that 8 cents per pound duty is of any benefit to our dairy farmers to-day. I will give them a chance and will take my seat
till they reply. I do not see any hon. gentleman get up to contradict me, and I will proceed. So that you have proof there that our policy was right and that of hon gentlemen opposite wrong. The fact is that our export business to New Zealand has been very nearly wiped out. In April, 1929-30, we exported to that country produce to the value of $1,105,220, while in April of 1931-32 our exports amounted to only $355,756-that is, for that month alone. That represent a loss of almost $1,000,000 a month.
What government was it that cancelled the agreement with New Zealand?

It was not the cancellation of the agreement but the imposition of the duty that had the effect of wiping out that business. It was during the short session that the 8 cents duty was put on, and the moment this was done New Zealand retaliated by discontinuing all trade with us except such as they were bound to carry on.

To my hon. friends on this side I have an even more painful duty to perform, because I find several hon. members on this side still think the National Dairy Council is a political organization. What have they got against the National Dairy Council when they asked simply that the original duty be restored and Mr. Dunning restored it and introduced it in his budget? W7e fought the election on it. It came too late, though, and was grossly misrepresented by our opponents. But we should not blame the National Daily Council for that.
I think we should be quite candid with each other and be fair to all parties. I know 
the National Dairy Council. The first time I ever raised my voice in this house was on the question of oleomargarine, which is quite a proper subject to discuss under this appropriation. I got a really good spanking from my own side that night and I felt it too. But the National Dairy Council got into the fight. Without it we would not have won, and even at that it took us two years to abolish this abomination, this unfair competition with the dairymen of Canada, a product that is now being fought by the dairy industry in the United States. Therefore I shall never forget the good work of the National Dairy Council from that date to this, and all their boards of directors, none of which had a more capable head than the present one, Mr. Robinson, an exceptionally efficient gentleman. This would go out with the cheques.

In view of the above conditions it is necessary to reduce cream prices, which are as follows: Table, 27 cents; Special, 25 cents.

continue if I may, because I have been very quiet all afternoon. Has the Minister of Agriculture the figures for 1922 and 1923 that were asked for?

I surely shall not be accused of any immodesty when I point out that it was not the agricultural statistics that had to be changed at all. I was aware of the difference between the two sets of figures ever since I came down here, and on many occasions I spoke to my then deputy about it and took the ground, as he did, that some reconciliation should be made between the two sets of figures by the respective departments, Agriculture and Trade and Commerce, instead of having two even slightly conflicting sets going out to the country. There was not very much difference between them, but the difference that did exist just gave the opportunity to such hon. gentlemen as the hon. member for South Hastings .to get up and say what he did

I may say quite frankly that I did not know that the matter had been adjusted. With regard to these milk production figures, they correspond with the ones that I gave three or four days ago, and as the minister has intimated, they are as correct as any figures can possibly be; they are just as correct as any other figures the minister knows of, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce acquiesces in that. So we will all kind of lack thumbs on that point. There is no use in all this talk if we do not get somewhere by way of suggestions for betterment. Perhaps I cannot do better than repeat what I said on the 5th of May. I took the ground then, and I take it now, that our dairymen are absolutely up against it producing cheese and butter in these small factories throughout Canada at the present ruinous prices. The minister himself has pointed out the advantage of larger manufacturing units. He pointed to the men in Saskatchewan who started larger units there, and perhaps unintentionally he paid a compliment to the first government in that province. They have one of these larger units in Regina, one in Saskatoon, one in my hon. friends own constituency, possibly two, and the people there all know the advantages of these larger units. I know it too, because for ten years the Saskatchewan government operated a cooperative creamery which came under my personal observation, and although all my life I have been a farmer I have been incidentally an overseer of such a creamery, and in that way I happen to have a knowledge of the business which has been most invaluable to me all through my life. We all know theoretically that volume means a iower cost of production, but when you learn it in actual experience you know it in an altogether different way. Our dairymen are to-day at a great disadvantage in having the small manufacturing units for butter and cheese. Speaking on the 5th of May on the advantage of having a system of standardized creameries and dual purpose factories for butter and cheese, I said:
Our opponents, rivals, competitors, all over the world for the last twenty-five years have 
been gradually developing and enlarging the manufacturing units of their dairy products and increasing the production of the production unit, the cow, increasing the flow of her milk and increasing the size of the dairy buildings until they are eight or ten times as large as they were fifty or sixty years ago when dairy and cheese factories were started in Ontario. That has been going on for twenty-five years in the United States, New Zealand, Denmark and Russia. Our present dairy commissioner was the chief resident factor and adviser in starting up the present dairy industry in New Zealand. Doctor Ruddick knows all about these plants, and of what advantage it is to have a large production in each one, which tends not only to quality and cheapness of production but to uniformity of product, which is so acceptable on the markets of any country. In our own country, through the effluxion of time, the old junk factories, which were all right at the beginning, are disappearing, and better ones are taking their place; but if we leave it to the process of evolution I am afraid it will take us about a hundred years before we can compete successfully in dairy products with our competitors throughout the world. We can compete now% yes, but it is a competition that leaves our dairyman skinned right dowrn to the heels; there is nothing left for him at all, with cheese at nine cents and butter at twenty and twenty-two cents a pound. They need government help; and let the government take action now. The thought I have in mind now' is what I had in mind when I w'as minister and when $25,000 was put in the estimates of 1930 for a live stock inquiry; and it looks even better now than it did then, because this government is committed as no previous government ever was to putting the whole weight and pow-er of this dominion behind agriculture, as was promised at the last election.
This is the time to strike. The only thing the minister had to say in reply was that this was not the time to make a move in that direction. May I be excused for differing? I believe that this surely is the very time to make the move. There is an old saying that we should strike when the iron is hot, and I think the iron is pretty hot now all over Canada with respect to the dairy industry, and now would be a splended time to strike. The government I know can only go as far as public opinion will permit, and I believe that the public would be wholly behind the government in taking any move along the line I suggested. I went on to say:
My good friend the Minister of Agriculture can ask for almost anything from this government for agriculture, and if he secures it I can assure him that he will have a solid phalanx of this side of the house behind him too. It is said that w'e sometimes play politics, but in view of the present distressing conditions in the w'est, the member of parliament who plays politics alone will not last very long. They want us to be big enough to stand up and help the government in anything that will be of benefit to agriculture, even though we oppose the general policies of the government.

Hon. members must know that at the present time it is quite popular to talk about vague policies, but Mr. Robinson's was apparently a reality, though not yet available. The Hon. Robert Weir is aware of all these things.

In dairying he believed it to be of prime necessity that we first fully supply our own home market.

Then the address continues:

In that connection Mr. Robinson refers to the council. But what did they promise? They promised to put the whole weight and power of the Dominion of Canada

Is technical education any more important than the dairy industry? I wonder how many hon. gentlemen ever got up at half past four in the morning to milk cows.
I have.

Then the hon.
member ought to be sympathetic. But he did not do so when cheese was at 8 cents a pound; that is lower than the price when he was a boy. Well, there will now be a little bond of friendship between the two of us. Dairying is a very arduous branch of agriculture, as everybody knows, I think. It is weakening right now at the knees, it is being hard-pressed, although it is the only source from which there is any available money just now. Wheat has gone up the flue for a while, and I do not know how long it will stay up there, but every old cow that can be milked at all, her udder has to be stripped so as to secure the very last squirt of milk in order that we may scrape along.
Oh, oh.

I am not joking.
We farmer members know that. It is what we are living on to-day. The only trouble is that we have not enough of those life saving cows. I have heard it said that the Prime Minister has no heart; or if he has, he has not been able to diagnose the ills of the west, and therefore cannot prescribe a remedy. My hon. friend is a western man. We are proud to know that the ministers of agriculture are coming from the west, whether from the far west or from the middle west. The present minister knows conditions, he knows what dairying is. Would it be so very difficult for him to put up a scrap for the same grant that technical education got? It would not take that much for the first year. Suppose only $100,000 was put in the supplementaries to have an inquiry. I asked for only $25,000 last year. Quadruple that and see if something cannot be done. [DOT] The minister has a very good committee here. I think that that is not an unreasonable request, and I say with all sincerity that this is the time to strike. There is not a man in this house who would dare to object to a policy to be enunciated for the purpose of rehabilitating our dairy industry and establishing a standardized system of combined creameries and dairies, especially in the two
older provinces of Ontario and Quebec as a start-up. With that will go the two packing plants that were suggested. If ever I spoke a sincere word in my life I am speaking it now. It is not usual for the opposition to advocate a policy so transparently necessary that scarcely any government could resist it, and then give them the opportunity to run away with it. I do not care if you run from here to you-know-where with it, so long as we get a rejuvenated dairy industry. I am willing to give credit for it to the Hon. Martin Burrell who preceded me, or to any of my other predecessors, so long as something is done to revivify agriculture, especially on the prairies.
Some unkind things have been said about the prairies. Yes, we are making quite a noise. You will never get anything in this world without you do make a certain amount of noise; but we have not got much out there yet this session. What we have got you could pretty well put in your eye and not interfere with your vision. But it will come, and it has to come from this government. Could not the minister take advantage of the opportunity, and come out with a flourish as the great emancipator of agrioulture in the west-instead of blaming me for weeds that grew thirteen years ago when I was not there. What was done at that time at Waterhen Lake was done by the Tory government that preceded us. Oh, the need must have been great for my hon. friend to seek to blame me, and I am sure he regrets it now. How much better would this proposition be than that which he advocated in his recent speech- a speech which reechoed throughout Canada as a victorious vindication of the minister for twenty-three minutes, and then collapsed. The other day I asked the Minister of Agriculture concerning our butter, and he said at that time that we were nearly on an export basis. I have given notice that at this meeting the chief item on the agenda will be a national dairy policy for Canada.

If we want to export them they must be produced in steady and dependable supply of high and uniform quality, and above all at prices low enough to enable us to compete with other countries.
In other words, he says that we are assembled here to-day at this convention in order to work out a policy; we are on an export basis for butter, or soon will be; we must have a steady supply of uniform quality, and it is up to us and the government to work out such a policy. Now, what has the government done toward working out a policy along that line? Are -they doing anything in order -that we may have a steady supply of butter of uniform quality? Are they doing anything in order to reduce the cost of producing butter? These small creameries, we have been told, produce butter at a high cost, and, as has just been pointed out, we should have larger units. What are the government doing to increase the size of these creameries?

subtopic: ALGOMA CENTRAL AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
There is rather a long preamble attached to this bill, and possibly a short explanation would facilitate its passing. The purpose of the bill is to confirm a certain "scheme of arrangement" that has been agreed to between the Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway Company, the Algoma Central Terminals Limited, the bondholders of both these companies and the Lake Superior Corporation which guarantees the bonds. It is, in short, a reorganization
[The Chairman.]
of the financial structure of these companies. The companies are part of the industrial institutions that were established by Mr. F. H. Clergue some years ago at Sault Ste. Marie. The Lake Superior Corporation is not an operating company; it might be termed a holding company. The Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway Company, the Algoma Central Terminals Limited and the Algoma Steel Corporation, the subsidiary companies, are the operating companies.
The railway has been built for a distance of some 296 miles north from Sault Ste. Marie, with a branch running from a place called Hawk junction to Michipicoten harbour. It taps the main line of the Canadian Pacific at Franz, the Canadian National, formerly the Canadian Northern, at a place called Oba, and the Grand Trunk Pacific at Hearst, and it really forms the only means whereby the Canadian National can connect with the industries at Sault Ste. Marie.
For the purpose of raising money for the construction of the railway, it was necessary to issue first mortgage bonds. These bonds were guaranteed by the parent company, the Lake Superior Corporation, and the purpose in mind in the construction of the railway was not only to freight pulpwood down to the pulp and paper mill which was at that time a subsidiary of this company known as the Lake Superior Pulp and Paper Company and now owned by the Abitibi people, but to move iron ore from the then Helen mine to the blast furnaces to be constructed at Sault Ste. Marie. Unfortunately the railway was not able to earn sufficient money to pay the interest on the bonds. Much of the pulpwood was of course floated down by water, and the old Helen mine, from which they mined merchantable ore, petered out, with the result that in 1916 the Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway passed into the hands of a receiver. At that time an arrangement was arrived at, satisfactory to the Lake Superior Corporation and to the shareholders and bondholders of the railway company, whereby the road was returned to the original owners and an act of this parliament was passed approving the arrangement then made. It was thought that the prospects for the future were better. It was known there were large deposits of low grade iron ore, and it was hoped they would be able to treat this ore and use it in their blast furnaces. This would have provided considerable traffic for the railway. The Algoma Steel Corporation spent some $2,500,000 in erecting a plant at what was known as the Magpie mine for treating or beneficiating this low

Private Bills
grade ore. They proved that this ore could be successfully treated and made fit for blast furnace use, but the methods then known for treating this ore were not as advanced as they are to-day.

subtopic: ALGOMA CENTRAL AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: It was magnetite ore they were treating at that time. They have hematite, magnetite and siderite. But the cost of the treatment of the ore was such that they were not able to treat it and lay it down at the blast furnaces as cheaply as they could purchase iron ore elsewhere. The result has been that the railway company has not been able so far to earn sufficient money to pay more than the operating expenses and a very small amount on the interest on the bonds. By the way, since 1916 the railway companies have paid out about $15,000,000 in wages. It is realized that the only hope lies in the successful operation of the steel industry at Sault Ste. Marie. Consequently they agreed to enter into an arrangement whereby the Lake Superior Corporation would be relieved of their guarantee of the bonds, which would enable them to go on to the market and more successfully finance the extensions to the steel industry which are absolutely necessary in order to enable that industry more successfully to meet the demands for steel in the Dominion of Canada. This arrangement has been approved by the bondholders, by the shareholders of the Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway Company, the Algoma Central Terminals Limited and the shareholders of the Lake Superior Corporation. It is practically a family affair, to which all the members have given their assent, and all these industries being situated in the province of Ontario approval has been given by a bill passed by the legislature of that province at its recent session. The bill before us, as hon. members will observe has also been considered and passed by the upper chamber of this parliament.

Perhaps I should have explained in my earlier remarks that the parent company, the Lake Superior Corporation, was originally incorporated under the laws of the state of New Jersey. Under the proposed arrangement a new holding company is to be set up to be known as the Algoma Consolidated Corporation Limited, a Canadian company. The American trustees have been changed to Canadian trustees, and the shareholders of the former company have to the extent of over 90 per cent given their approval by turning in their shares to be exchanged for shares in this new holding company. The question may be asked, what about the remaining ten per cent? Some of this stock was held in the old land and in other parts of Europe, and as no dividends have been paid on the stock since it was first issued over thirty years ago, it is possible that some of these shares have been misplaced or lost. I doubt if there are very many members of this house who, holding stock on which they have received no dividends for a period of fifteen or twenty years, have been very much interested in taking care of the certificates. That is the explanation.

Yes-it is good reading. But on election day we found the real reason for the whole thing. I say I am not blaming the government of the day; I am blaming the political manoeuverers in that part of the country, for what did they do? They learned a lesson in 1917, they learned how to distribute votes and how to win that war time election, so all these people were not allowed to vote. There were Ontario government aeroplanes to bring out those who they knew would vote right, and they voted by perjury and fraud in the rural polls. Over one hundred voters were brought out I am advised by the campaign managers and they voted in the rural polls, under section 232 of the Dominion Elections Act, under which a person has only to vouch that the person is a 
resident of the district. They are permitted to vote, notwithstanding the fact that they are not on the voters' list. That was the real reasdn, and now the government introduces an amendment, after I introduced this bill to enfranchise these people, and if that amendment is adopted it will practically keep those people disfranchised.
I am sorry the Minister of Justice was not leading the house on that occasion, because I believe his fairness would have made this further debate unnecessary. I am satisfied that the real Conservatives did not wish these six hundred miners, pioneers of this country, and especially in Ontario, disfranchised, and I am satisfied that the Minister of Justice would not be a party to such political manoeuvering. He would not have agreed to the sending in of aeroplanes in order to bring out these people to vote at rural polls by fraud and perjury. Through this amendment, however, that is what the government is subscribing to at the present time.
I do not wish to labour this question. Had the Minister of Justice been in his seat I am satisfied he would have spoken a little differently than the way the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke. I think probably he would have said this was a proper bill to be introduced, but that inasmuch as a redistribution may take place before the next election, the government would give the assurance that before any election took place they would see to it that these people were given the franchise. I am certain of that, but instead the Minister of Trade and Commerce rises in his seat and calls the measure everything but its right name. He has indicated by his language that it is silly, that a person could not be sincere in introducing it at this time. He has talked about rumours and all that sort of thing, which have nothing to do with the bill. He has moved an amendment Which, if carried, will have the effect of keeping the franchise from these people until some other step may be taken.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to dwell upon the quertion further. I am satisfied that the house will not accept the amendment of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I certainly hope that will not be the case because we will be simply giving an impetus and an encouragement to a few-I will say not more than six-political manipulators, who never did anything for the district or for the Conservative party. They will be able to work in conjunction with a few politicians in the city of Toronto in order to keep these six hundred people as a reserve upon which

Representation Act
they may draw in the event of being hard pressed during an election.
Talking about political manoeuvering, these people were actually encouraged by some of the ministers of the provincial government to do these things. By the way, I see questions on the order paper indicating that people were dismissed because of partisanship in provincial and federal elections. We had the spectacle in our constituency of the defeated candidate working in conjunction with the officers of the Ontario government, road foremen and engineers, on election day, bring in the voters on government trucks, off the highways. They stood one on each side of the sidewalk with the pay list, calling these people by numbers. The candidate would say, "number so-and-so, you are working for us out at camp so-and-so, and it is your duty to vote, step in this way." These people were used for the purpose of winning one seat, but notwithstanding all that, the Conservative did not make the grade. In fact, if it had not been for the Ontario government and their methods of bribeiy, corruption, intimidation and persecution of the settlers, they would not have reached first base during the last election. All that I am asking to do by this bill is to enfranchise these six hundred people and let them vote as they will at the next election.

Yet he comes forward this session and complains of the wrongs done to the people in his own riding, when the whole blame in the matter rests on his own shoulders and on the shoulders of the government of which he was a member which failed to pass the bill. He says that the government was not in power during the election in 1926. I agree. But it was in power in 1927, and he was a member of it. It was in power in 1928 and he was a member of it. It was in power in 1929 and again in 1930, and he was a member of that government. For four long years this crying outrage which he has pictured to-night continued in his own territory and he did not raise a hand to redress it. In 1930 he did take some steps in the matter, but some influence was brought to bear upon him, because he allowed the government of which he was a member, to abandon bis bill. He allowed the house to adjourn without passing the measure. He apparently thinks that the minority of the House of Commons should have put the bill through. He was in the government until election day, 1930, and failed to afford the right to vote to these good people.
Such is the ridiculous position in which the hon. member finds himself to-night. And this is the sort of proposal he submits to the House of Commons. What is the answer? It is a simple one. This is the first session of a new parliament. Under the constitution of the country, the census must be taken this year. As soon as the census is taken the constitution prescribes that a redistribution of the ridings shall take place. Surely this matter can wait one year. This government will be in power another year; we can guarantee the hon. gentleman that. When the redistribution bill comes down the matter will be righted. But why interject a measure of this kind at this session? There is nothing to be gained thereby. The hon. gentleman did not do it when he had power, but now he projects this bill as a grievance to parade in the north country to induce the people to believe that he has been working to get them votes now that he

It had not been my intention to participate in the debate on this bill, but when the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) rises in his place and makes the allegations which he does as allegations of fact as to what occurred in the district of Patricia in 1926, I wish, in the strongest terms of which I am capable, to deny these allegations; because in 1926 I was the magistrate of the district of Patricia. As that district was at that time, and still is, an unorganized territory, I had charge of the administration of justice, including the direction of the provincial police officers in the district of Patricia. When the proclamation was issued for the election of 1926, there was not a parliament in session and consequently the question as to whether or not the people then resident in that district should have a vote was a matter dependent upon the statutes. Some of the permanent residents, few in number as they still are, desired to have a poll established in that district and application was made therefor to the returning officer for >the adjoining district of Kenora-Rainy River. Apparently for a short period of time the local returning officer for that district was under the impression thet. he would be able to grant a poll in the district of Patricia. But the chief electoral officer for Canada, or his legal adviser, I am not sure which, overruled the decision of the local returning officer. Hence a poll was not established in the district.
Before hon. members vote on this measure I should like to place before them another little picture so that it will not appear that vast numbers of the permanent residents of this country are being disfranchised. The district of Patricia is a vast, unsettled, un-

organized area. In order to proceed from Hudson on the national railway to the first settlement-that is, apart from Indians-at the Hudson bay post at lac Seul, you have to journey 127 miles by canoe at most times of the year and, sometimes when the Manitou rapids are high, you can go in a launch. It takes two mighty good paddlers three days to make the trip. At Gold Pines, which is a local centre, there were in 1926 fourteen permanent residents, and in the summer of 1930 there were not more than forty-two. That, I believe, was my count when I journeyed there at that time. To the next settlement in that country, which is the Howie mine, where a number of men are working-that is, at Red lake-it is seventy miles by water, with six portages. That was the number originally, but at the present time, I believe, by the flooding of the upper and lower Ear falls by the provincial hydro development two of the short portages have been eliminated. You cannot travel by launch because you cannot take a launch over the portages; so that, again, it takes twTo very good paddlers, as I know very wrell, to paddle a canoe and make the partages from Howie mines at Red lake, a matter of three days, to get to the town-site of Gold Pines. The very best you can do it in is two days. There is a small settlement consisting of about four permanent residents at Jackson-Manion mines, and to get there you have to go ninety miles by canoe, with eleven portages, two of them a mile and a quarter long. There are few facilities for transportation in that country, so that you. are not disfranchising any enormous number of people when you fail to pass this bill at this session.

A few minutes before six o'clock I had asked the Minister of Agriculture a question with regard to the National Dairy Council, when the hon. member who at that moment was acting as chairman ruled me out of order. I want to revert to that question. I asked the minister also if >he had any knowledge of the movement on foot to merge all the small creameries of this country into a gigantic monopoly whereby the farmer would lose a large amount of
his revenue and the consumer would be forced to pay an exorbitant price for butter, cheese, cream, milk and all other produce allied to the dairy industry. The minister replied that he had no knowledge of such a merger. I want to ask him a further question and I think the committee and the country are entitled to the information before this item passes, because in my judgment this is a vital matter. Will he take steps to investigate and find out whether there is anything in the rumour that this merger is under way? While he is doing that, I should like him to find out, because I think it is his duty to do so, whether or not any of the officials of the National Dairy Council are interested in the merger of these creameries, whether they are soliciting stock subscriptions from the farmers and the people generally for this merger in order that they may wipe out the individual and cooperative creameries and get the whole dairy industry under their own control. Will the minister give his assurance to the committee that he will investigate and find out whether there is anything to this rumour, and also whether some of the officers of the National Dairy Council are interested in the merger? I shall ask the minister for his reply and I want to tell the chairman that if the minister answers my question now, I intend to continue my remarks.

I shall answer the hon. member's
question before I conclude the remarks which I am about to make. The hon. member for Willow Bunch, before the six o'clock recess of the committee, asked me to make a statement in connection with the dairy policy that I am endeavouring to formulate for the benefit of the dairy industry. I think that was a very fair question and quite in order at this particular time. As regards the reference he made, requesting that I make a statement in reference to the national dairy policy as discussed by the National Dairy Council at their conference in Winnipeg, I may say that the details of that entire policy are not yet worked out. There was a misunderstanding regarding the request that I made of the president of the National Dairy Council before he proceeded to the Winnipeg conference. I asked him to bring up unofficially before this conference, certain points in connection with an advocated daily policy, but not to bring the matter up as part of a dairy policy. What I wanted was to get the opinion or the reaction, with as little prejudice as possible, of those people who were-

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
there, representative as they were of various phases of the dairy industry. The president of the National Dairy Council evidently misunderstood me. He understood me to ask him to bring up this dairy policy of which we had the skeleton and which we had not had time to submit to a number of people to whom I had hoped to submit it before that time. I think it is only fair to him to say that due to the pressure of work to which I have had to give attention, the misunderstanding is more likely to have been on my part than on his. It was not intended by me that that should be presented to the conference as the skeleton of a national dairy policy, although I do not claim that anything he said was not correct. What he did say was quite correct.
As I said at the outset, the policy is not worked out in detail. I think it is only fair that, as has been requested, I should outline to the committee as much of the dairy policy as we have in view and some of which we have already put into practice. I think we can agree that in any dairy policy which we formulate the ideal that any dairyman would have in mind is something of this nature: to produce dairy products,-let us take for illustration butter-to produce dairy butter of such a quality that it will compete, favourably with butter put on the world market from any other dairy farmer in the world; not only that, but to produce it at the lowest possible cost and to have it marketed in such a way that thea-e will be returned to the dairyman the highest possible portion of what the consumer pays for it.
